15:T30c9,<p>I needed to deploy a Go HTTP server on AWS. Docker build, push, run — three commands on my machine. On AWS, those three commands turned into a maze of Task Definitions, Capacity Providers, Services, and Target Groups.</p>
<p>Here's what actually happened.</p>
<hr>
<h2>The Docker part is easy</h2>
<p>If you know Docker, you already know 80% of this. Build. Tag. Push. The only difference is the registry URL.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">docker</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> build</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> -t</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> my-app</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> .</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">docker</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> tag</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> my-app:latest</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">docker</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> push</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Two more steps to run it:</p>
<ol>
<li>Create a Task Definition in ECS — point it to <code>123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest</code></li>
<li>Launch a Service or Task — pick the task definition and run</li>
</ol>
<p>Done. The rest of this article is about what went wrong between those steps.</p>
<hr>
<h2>The Go build that broke silently</h2>
<p>A normal multi-stage Dockerfile:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="dockerfile" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="dockerfile" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">FROM</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> golang:1.22 </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">AS</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> builder</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">WORKDIR</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> /app</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">COPY</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> go.mod go.sum ./</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">RUN</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> go mod download</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">COPY</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> . .</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">RUN</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -a -installsuffix cgo -o main .</span></span>
<span data-line=""> </span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">FROM</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> alpine:latest</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">RUN</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> apk --no-cache add ca-certificates</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">WORKDIR</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> /root/</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">COPY</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> --from=builder /app/main .</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">CMD</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> [</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"./main"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">]</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Two flags matter here.</p>
<h3>CGO_ENABLED=0</h3>
<p>Go has its own implementations for low-level operations — networking, DNS, crypto. Setting <code>CGO_ENABLED=0</code> tells the compiler: use those pure Go implementations. Don't link against the system's C library.</p>
<p>Without this, the binary depends on the exact glibc version in your build environment. Alpine uses musl, not glibc. The binary crashes at startup with a cryptic shared library error.</p>
<p>Trade-off: pure Go implementations are slightly larger but run anywhere. If your code needs C interop (SQLite, some graphics libraries), set it to <code>1</code> and match your base image's C library.</p>
<h3>GOARCH=amd64</h3>
<p>ECS Fargate only supports two architectures: <code>X86_64</code> and <code>ARM64</code>. The default is <code>X86_64</code>.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>"If the property is undefined, <code>operatingSystemFamily</code> is <code>LINUX</code> and <code>cpuArchitecture</code> is <code>X86_64</code>" — <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/python/aws_cdk.aws_ecs_patterns/FargateServiceBaseProps.html">AWS CDK FargateServiceBaseProps</a></p>
</blockquote>
<p>If you build on an M1/M2 Mac without specifying <code>GOARCH</code>, Go defaults to <code>arm64</code> — because Go cross-compilation targets the host architecture by default. The image pushes to ECR fine. Fargate pulls it fine. Then:</p>
<pre><code>exec ./main: exec format error
</code></pre>
<p>The binary is <code>arm64</code>, but Fargate's runtime is <code>X86_64</code>. Architecture mismatch. Specify <code>GOARCH=amd64</code> (or <code>arm64</code> if you chose ARM64 in Task Definition).</p>
<blockquote>
<p>"When you register a task definition, you specify the CPU architecture. The valid values are <code>X86_64</code> and <code>ARM64</code>." Default: <code>X86_64</code> — <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html">Amazon ECS task definition parameters</a></p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h2>Capacity Provider: why two things exist for "just pick Fargate"</h2>
<p>When you create a Service, ECS asks: Launch Type or Capacity Provider Strategy?</p>
<p><strong>Launch Type</strong> is simple. Pick Fargate, EC2, or Fargate Spot. Done.</p>
<p><strong>Capacity Provider Strategy</strong> exists because production deployments need cost optimization. You mix Fargate (reliable, expensive) with Fargate Spot (cheap, might get interrupted). Two parameters control the mix:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>base</code> — guaranteed minimum tasks for one provider. One provider's base must be 0.</li>
<li><code>weight</code> — ratio for distributing the remaining tasks.</li>
</ul>
<p>Example: 12 tasks, Fargate base=3, Spot base=0, weights 1:2.</p>

























<table><thead><tr><th></th><th>Fargate</th><th>Fargate Spot</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>base</td><td>3</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><td>weight</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>result</td><td>6 (3 + 3)</td><td>6 (0 + 6)</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>First, Fargate gets its base of 3. Nine tasks remain. Weight 1:2 splits them 3 and 6. Fargate: 6 total. Spot: 6 total.</p>
<p>This matters for Services. Tasks don't auto-scale, so the strategy only affects initial placement.</p>
<hr>
<h2>Service or Task: the choice that confused me</h2>
<p>I assumed Service and Task were fundamentally different things. They're not.</p>
<p><strong>Tasks are the actual running units.</strong> Every container you run on ECS is a Task. Always.</p>
<p><strong>Services are a management layer on top of Tasks.</strong> A Service says "keep N tasks running" and adds auto-scaling, load balancing, and rolling deployments.</p>
<p>When I created a Service with 3 replicas, I expected to see one Service. Instead, I saw one Service and three Tasks. The Service didn't replace Tasks — it created them.</p>





















<table><thead><tr><th>ECS</th><th>Kubernetes equivalent</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Task</td><td>Pod</td></tr><tr><td>Service</td><td>Deployment + Service</td></tr><tr><td>Task Definition</td><td>Pod spec</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>For a long-running HTTP server: Service. For a one-time batch job, CI/CD step, or cron: Task.</p>
<p>Here's what surprised me: the console lets you switch between Service and Task configurations freely. Choose "Run new Task," then change settings to look like a Service. The options are almost identical — Service just adds auto-scaling and ALB integration. The UI separation is for user clarity, not a technical boundary.</p>
<p>Even the Task Definition's launch type setting isn't binding. Define it as EC2, then launch it as Fargate. ECS doesn't enforce the match.</p>
<hr>
<h2>ALB: why you want it even for a single server</h2>
<p>Without ALB, your task gets a public IP. That IP changes every time the task restarts. Users can't bookmark it. You can't add HTTPS.</p>
<p>ALB solves this through target groups. ECS registers tasks into a target group. ALB routes traffic to the target group. You expose one stable DNS name.</p>
<p>Multiple services, one ALB:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>domain.app/api</code> → target group <code>backend</code></li>
<li><code>domain.app/</code> → target group <code>landing-page</code></li>
</ul>
<p>When you create a Service, the Load Balancing section lets you assign a target group. That's the registration step — ECS tells ALB "send traffic to these tasks."</p>
<h3>From ALB to HTTPS with a custom domain</h3>
<p>Three steps:</p>
<ol>
<li>Add an HTTPS listener on port 443. Attach your domain's ACM certificate.</li>
<li>Set the HTTP listener on port 80 to redirect to HTTPS.</li>
<li>In Route53, create an A record alias pointing your domain to the ALB's DNS name.</li>
</ol>
<p>Custom domain. HTTPS. No certificates to manage on the server.</p>
<p>One trap hides here: if the load balancer returns 502 even though the task itself works, the target group's protocol is almost always the cause. I wrote that one up separately in <a href="/v2/alb-502-target-group-protocol">why my load balancer returned 502</a>.</p>
<hr>
<h2>What I'd do differently</h2>
<p>Task Definition is to ECS what AMI is to EC2 — a blueprint. But Task Definition is simpler. An AMI captures an entire OS, processes, and configurations. A Task Definition just describes containers, resource limits, and environment variables.</p>
<p>The key difference: Task Definition must exist before you create a Service or Task. AMI is optional — you can launch an EC2 instance from AWS's default AMIs.</p>
<p>If I set this up again:</p>
<ol>
<li>Start with Capacity Provider Strategy, not Launch Type. Even if you only use Fargate today, the migration path to Spot is painless.</li>
<li>Always specify <code>GOARCH</code>. Cross-compilation is free. Debugging format errors is not.</li>
<li>Put ALB in front from day one. The cost is minimal. Retrofitting HTTPS and stable DNS later is a headache.</li>
<li>Use Service, not Task, for anything that should stay running. The auto-restart alone is worth it.</li>
</ol>
<hr>
<h2>References</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/">Docker multi-platform builds</a></li>
<li><a href="https://gist.github.com/asukakenji/f15ba7e588ac42795f421b48b8aede63">Go cross-compilation flags</a></li>
<li><a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/73285601/docker-exec-usr-bin-sh-exec-format-error">exec format error — StackOverflow</a></li>
<li><a href="https://dev.to/metal3d/understand-how-to-use-c-libraries-in-go-with-cgo-3dbn">Using CGO in Go</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html">Amazon ECS task definition parameters for Fargate</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/python/aws_cdk.aws_ecs_patterns/FargateServiceBaseProps.html">AWS CDK FargateServiceBaseProps</a></li>
</ul>16:T1f2a,
I needed to deploy a Go HTTP server on AWS. Docker build, push, run — three commands on my machine. On AWS, those three commands turned into a maze of Task Definitions, Capacity Providers, Services, and Target Groups.

Here's what actually happened.

---

## The Docker part is easy

If you know Docker, you already know 80% of this. Build. Tag. Push. The only difference is the registry URL.

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker tag my-app:latest 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest
```

Two more steps to run it:

1. Create a Task Definition in ECS — point it to `123456789.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest`
2. Launch a Service or Task — pick the task definition and run

Done. The rest of this article is about what went wrong between those steps.

---

## The Go build that broke silently

A normal multi-stage Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -a -installsuffix cgo -o main .

FROM alpine:latest
RUN apk --no-cache add ca-certificates
WORKDIR /root/
COPY --from=builder /app/main .
CMD ["./main"]
```

Two flags matter here.

### CGO_ENABLED=0

Go has its own implementations for low-level operations — networking, DNS, crypto. Setting `CGO_ENABLED=0` tells the compiler: use those pure Go implementations. Don't link against the system's C library.

Without this, the binary depends on the exact glibc version in your build environment. Alpine uses musl, not glibc. The binary crashes at startup with a cryptic shared library error.

Trade-off: pure Go implementations are slightly larger but run anywhere. If your code needs C interop (SQLite, some graphics libraries), set it to `1` and match your base image's C library.

### GOARCH=amd64

ECS Fargate only supports two architectures: `X86_64` and `ARM64`. The default is `X86_64`.

> "If the property is undefined, `operatingSystemFamily` is `LINUX` and `cpuArchitecture` is `X86_64`" — [AWS CDK FargateServiceBaseProps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/python/aws_cdk.aws_ecs_patterns/FargateServiceBaseProps.html)

If you build on an M1/M2 Mac without specifying `GOARCH`, Go defaults to `arm64` — because Go cross-compilation targets the host architecture by default. The image pushes to ECR fine. Fargate pulls it fine. Then:

```
exec ./main: exec format error
```

The binary is `arm64`, but Fargate's runtime is `X86_64`. Architecture mismatch. Specify `GOARCH=amd64` (or `arm64` if you chose ARM64 in Task Definition).

> "When you register a task definition, you specify the CPU architecture. The valid values are `X86_64` and `ARM64`." Default: `X86_64` — [Amazon ECS task definition parameters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html)

---

## Capacity Provider: why two things exist for "just pick Fargate"

When you create a Service, ECS asks: Launch Type or Capacity Provider Strategy?

**Launch Type** is simple. Pick Fargate, EC2, or Fargate Spot. Done.

**Capacity Provider Strategy** exists because production deployments need cost optimization. You mix Fargate (reliable, expensive) with Fargate Spot (cheap, might get interrupted). Two parameters control the mix:

- `base` — guaranteed minimum tasks for one provider. One provider's base must be 0.
- `weight` — ratio for distributing the remaining tasks.

Example: 12 tasks, Fargate base=3, Spot base=0, weights 1:2.

| | Fargate | Fargate Spot |
|---|---|---|
| base | 3 | 0 |
| weight | 1 | 2 |
| result | 6 (3 + 3) | 6 (0 + 6) |

First, Fargate gets its base of 3. Nine tasks remain. Weight 1:2 splits them 3 and 6. Fargate: 6 total. Spot: 6 total.

This matters for Services. Tasks don't auto-scale, so the strategy only affects initial placement.

---

## Service or Task: the choice that confused me

I assumed Service and Task were fundamentally different things. They're not.

**Tasks are the actual running units.** Every container you run on ECS is a Task. Always.

**Services are a management layer on top of Tasks.** A Service says "keep N tasks running" and adds auto-scaling, load balancing, and rolling deployments.

When I created a Service with 3 replicas, I expected to see one Service. Instead, I saw one Service and three Tasks. The Service didn't replace Tasks — it created them.

| ECS | Kubernetes equivalent |
|---|---|
| Task | Pod |
| Service | Deployment + Service |
| Task Definition | Pod spec |

For a long-running HTTP server: Service. For a one-time batch job, CI/CD step, or cron: Task.

Here's what surprised me: the console lets you switch between Service and Task configurations freely. Choose "Run new Task," then change settings to look like a Service. The options are almost identical — Service just adds auto-scaling and ALB integration. The UI separation is for user clarity, not a technical boundary.

Even the Task Definition's launch type setting isn't binding. Define it as EC2, then launch it as Fargate. ECS doesn't enforce the match.

---

## ALB: why you want it even for a single server

Without ALB, your task gets a public IP. That IP changes every time the task restarts. Users can't bookmark it. You can't add HTTPS.

ALB solves this through target groups. ECS registers tasks into a target group. ALB routes traffic to the target group. You expose one stable DNS name.

Multiple services, one ALB:

- `domain.app/api` → target group `backend`
- `domain.app/` → target group `landing-page`

When you create a Service, the Load Balancing section lets you assign a target group. That's the registration step — ECS tells ALB "send traffic to these tasks."

### From ALB to HTTPS with a custom domain

Three steps:

1. Add an HTTPS listener on port 443. Attach your domain's ACM certificate.
2. Set the HTTP listener on port 80 to redirect to HTTPS.
3. In Route53, create an A record alias pointing your domain to the ALB's DNS name.

Custom domain. HTTPS. No certificates to manage on the server.

One trap hides here: if the load balancer returns 502 even though the task itself works, the target group's protocol is almost always the cause. I wrote that one up separately in [why my load balancer returned 502](/v2/alb-502-target-group-protocol).

---

## What I'd do differently

Task Definition is to ECS what AMI is to EC2 — a blueprint. But Task Definition is simpler. An AMI captures an entire OS, processes, and configurations. A Task Definition just describes containers, resource limits, and environment variables.

The key difference: Task Definition must exist before you create a Service or Task. AMI is optional — you can launch an EC2 instance from AWS's default AMIs.

If I set this up again:

1. Start with Capacity Provider Strategy, not Launch Type. Even if you only use Fargate today, the migration path to Spot is painless.
2. Always specify `GOARCH`. Cross-compilation is free. Debugging format errors is not.
3. Put ALB in front from day one. The cost is minimal. Retrofitting HTTPS and stable DNS later is a headache.
4. Use Service, not Task, for anything that should stay running. The auto-restart alone is worth it.
